in.other_title: Closed QA without information asymmetry: debate vs direct QA depends on judge strength
in.rationale: Michael et al. say generalisation to reasoning or knowledge gaps beyond source-text access is unclear. Kenton et al. report that on closed tasks without information asymmetry debate beats consultancy but shows small or no benefit over direct QA for GPT-3.5 and Pro 1.0 judges; the judges are LLMs rather than humans.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate helps when the expertise gap is not just privileged access to a text, for closed QA with LLM judges

in.other_title: AI debate helps biased human judges assess controversial COVID-19 and climate claims
in.rationale: Michael et al. say debate is untested on political or ideologically charged issues and with judges holding strong priors. in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate's advantage over consultancy holds on ideologically charged claims with judges holding strong priors

text: The authors state that debate might behave differently on harder questions, on questions drawing on much larger bodies of scientific or domain knowledge, or on political, ethical or ideologically charged issues; that their judges start with no strong opinion, so robustness to strong prior views or biases like confirmation bias is untested; and that their expertise gap is only privileged access to a source text, so generalization to larger knowledge gaps or reasoning and persuasion skill gaps is unclear.
title: Limited setting: fiction QA, no strong judge priors, narrow information-only expertise gap
